study_material.title: Syllogisms - Complete Study Notes
study_material.introduction: Syllogisms give premises ('All A are B', 'Some B are C') and ask which conclusions follow with certainty. Draw Venn diagrams and accept a conclusion ONLY if it holds in every possible diagram consistent with the premises.
learning_objectives: Translate All/Some/No statements into Venn pictures
Chain two premises through the middle term
Reject conclusions that are merely possible

concepts.heading: 1. The Four Statement Types
concepts.body: All A are B (A inside B). No A is B (disjoint circles). Some A are B (overlap guaranteed). Some A are not B (part of A outside B). 'Some' means at least one - it says nothing about the rest.

concepts.heading: 2. Valid Chains
concepts.body: All A are B + All B are C gives All A are C. No A is B + All C are A gives No C is B. Some A are B guarantees Some B are A (conversion). All A are B converts only to Some B are A - never to All B are A.

concepts.heading: 3. The Certainty Test
concepts.body: A conclusion follows only if TRUE IN EVERY valid diagram. 'All roses are flowers; some flowers are red' does NOT give 'some roses are red' - the red flowers may all be non-roses. If you can draw one diagram where the conclusion fails, reject it.

concepts.heading: 4. Complementary Pairs
concepts.body: When neither of two conclusions follows individually but they exhaust all cases (e.g. 'Some A are B' / 'No A is B'), the answer is 'either I or II follows'. Look for this pattern when both conclusions involve the same terms.

formulas: All A are B: A inside B
Some A are B converts to Some B are A
All A are B converts to Some B are A only
Conclusion must survive every possible diagram
shortcut_methods: Draw the minimal diagram, then try to break each conclusion
'Some' + 'Some' premises almost never yield a definite conclusion
Check complementary either-or pairs before answering 'neither follows'
common_mistakes: Converting All A are B into All B are A
Accepting conclusions that are possible but not necessary
Importing real-world knowledge into abstract premises
study_material.summary: Venn-diagram the premises, test each conclusion against every consistent picture, and only certainty counts.
quick_revision_notes: All A are B + All B are C = All A are C
Either-or when conclusions exhaust the cases

solved_examples.question: Premises: All cats are animals. All animals are living beings. Conclusion: All cats are living beings. Does it follow?
solved_examples.step_by_step: Cats inside animals inside living beings - the chain is airtight.
solved_examples.shortcut: All + All chains through the middle term.

solved_examples.question: Premises: All roses are flowers. Some flowers are red. Conclusion: Some roses are red. Does it follow?
solved_examples.step_by_step: The red flowers might all be outside the rose circle. A diagram exists where no rose is red, so the conclusion is not certain.
solved_examples.shortcut: Some in the middle term proves nothing about the subset.

solved_examples.question: Premises: No dog is a cat. All puppies are dogs. Conclusion: No puppy is a cat. Does it follow?
solved_examples.step_by_step: Puppies sit inside dogs, and dogs are disjoint from cats - so puppies are disjoint from cats.
solved_examples.shortcut: Subset of a disjoint set is disjoint.

solved_examples.question: Premises: Some pens are pencils. Some pencils are erasers. Conclusion: Some pens are erasers. Does it follow?
solved_examples.step_by_step: The pencil-eraser overlap may avoid the pen-pencil overlap entirely. Some + Some yields no definite chain.

practice_questions.question: 'Some apples are fruits' can be validly converted to:
'All tigers are cats' validly yields which of these?
practice_questions.explanation: All A are B converts only partially: Some B are A.

practice_questions.question: Premises: All books are papers. No paper is plastic. Conclusion I: No book is plastic. Conclusion II: Some plastics are papers. Which follows?
practice_questions.explanation: Books inside papers, papers disjoint from plastic - I follows. II contradicts the premises.

practice_questions.question: Premises: Some doctors are singers. All singers are artists. Conclusion: Some doctors are artists. Does it follow?
practice_questions.explanation: The doctor-singer overlap sits inside artists, so those doctors are artists.

practice_questions.question: Premises: All A are B. Some B are C. Which conclusion definitely follows?
practice_questions.explanation: Only the conversion of the first premise is guaranteed; A-C relations are undetermined.

practice_questions.question: Premises: All keys are locks. Some locks are doors. Conclusions: I. Some keys are doors. II. No key is a door. Which follows?
practice_questions.explanation: Neither is certain, but the two exhaust all possibilities for keys and doors - the complementary pair.

practice_questions.question: Premises: All pens are tools. All tools are objects. Conclusions: I. All pens are objects. II. Some objects are pens. Which follows?
practice_questions.explanation: The chain gives I, and converting I gives II.

practice_questions.question: Premises: No fish is a bird. Some birds are swans. Conclusion: Some swans are not fish. Does it follow?
options: Only if all swans are birds
practice_questions.explanation: The swans that are birds cannot be fish (birds and fish are disjoint), so at least those swans are not fish.

topic_test.title: Syllogisms - Topic Test
instructions: +1 for correct, -0.25 for wrong, 0 for unattempted.
A conclusion follows only if no valid diagram can break it.

questions.question: All squares are rectangles. All rectangles are polygons. Therefore all squares are polygons. This argument is:
'No metal is a gas' converts validly to:
All A are B. No B is C. Conclusion: No A is C. Does it follow?
questions.explanation: A inside B, B disjoint from C.

questions.question: Some cars are trucks. All trucks are vehicles. Conclusions: I. Some cars are vehicles. II. All vehicles are trucks. Which follows?
questions.explanation: The overlap chains into vehicles; II reverses an All illegally.

questions.question: Some A are B. Some B are C. Conclusion: Some A are C. Does it follow?
questions.explanation: The overlaps may not intersect - classic Some+Some trap.

questions.question: All poets are dreamers. No dreamer is practical. Conclusions: I. No poet is practical. II. Some practical people are poets. Which follows?
questions.explanation: Chain gives I; II contradicts it.

questions.question: All X are Y. Conclusions: I. Some Y are X. II. Some Y are not X. Which follows?
questions.explanation: I is the valid partial conversion. II fails when X = Y exactly.

questions.question: No pin is a needle. All needles are sharp. Conclusions: I. Some sharp things are needles. II. No pin is sharp. Which follows?
questions.explanation: I converts premise 2. II is not forced - pins may be sharp without being needles.
